routes.name: Mac mini M6, 32 GB

routes.name: Raspberry Pi as the host for a desktop GPU
routes.memory: the card's own memory (20 GB RX 7900 XT, 24 GB RTX 4090, or 96 GB from four RTX A5000)
routes.price: $350 to $400 for the Pi side, plus the GPUs
routes.price_source: Jeff Geerling's own estimate for a Pi 5 or CM5 with an OCuLink dock, adapter and supply, Dec 2025; the Pi 500+ keyboard computer is $200. The GPUs are the real cost
measured: Pi 500+ with a Radeon RX 7900 XT over OCuLink (llama-bench, Vulkan): Llama 3.2 3B Q4_K_M 108.58 tok/s, Qwen2.5 14B Q4_K_M 7.16 tok/s, whole system about 315 to 330 W (Geerling, Sep 2025, read in full).

CM5 with an RTX 4090, llama.cpp Vulkan: Qwen3 30B less than 5% slower than a 265K desktop; small models and an AMD R9700 did much worse (Geerling, Dec 2025, read in full; the charts were not readable as text).
Four RTX A5000 on a Pi: Llama 3 70B 11.83 tok/s against 12 on an Intel server, a GitHub user's report relayed by Geerling; we did not open the original.
routes.watts: 315 to 330 W whole system with a 7900 XT
catches: The Pi is not what costs money and it saves little power: the whole system still draws 315 to 330 W under load.
It reached the PC's speed on NVIDIA cards that can pool memory directly through a PCIe 4 switch; mixed cards would not pool, AMD cards were flaky, and the amdgpu driver needed a 15-line kernel patch.
The x1 link is slow, so loading a model takes a while.
routes.verdict: A fun, documented experiment; not a cheaper way to 128 GB

routes.name: Modified NVIDIA cards with extra memory (2080 Ti 22 GB, 3080 20 GB, 4090 48 GB)
routes.price_source: Asking prices from several sellers and articles, mostly undated or from Oct to Nov 2026 (search excerpts and one page read in part); one shop quotes $4,989.99 for a finished 4090 48 GB
measured: One 2080 Ti 22 GB at 200 W: Gemma 4 26B-A4B 97 tok/s and Qwen3.6 27B 34 tok/s, self-reported on LinkedIn (Jul 2026, excerpt).

Capacity only: a 2080 Ti keeps its 616 GB/s bandwidth and has no FP8; running several over PCIe scales badly. Four 48 GB 4090s would be 192 GB for $13,000 to $16,000, which is not a budget route.
routes.verdict: Closest to the salvage spirit and the riskiest purchase here

egpu.intro: An external GPU lets a laptop or small PC you already own run a big model: the card holds the model, a dock connects it over USB4 or Thunderbolt, and a separate power supply feeds it. The first source below is one author, one set of machines and a patched Linux kernel, so read the speeds as what was seen there, not as a guarantee.
egpu.host_note: All speeds in this section were measured by the article's author on a 16-inch M1 Max MacBook Pro (NVIDIA and Intel cards) and a 14-inch M2 Max (the two AMD cards), running Omarchy with a patched 7.1.12 Linux kernel and local driver changes. The author says that is not a stock Omarchy recipe. We have not reproduced any of it.

egpu.fit_note: The 27B model fits on the 16 GB card with room to spare: weights 14,367 MiB, KV cache 661 MiB and compute buffer 150 MiB make 15,178 MiB on a card with 16,311 MiB, with all 66 layers on the card and 1,133 MiB free.
takeaways: The $299.99 RX 7600 decoded a 7B model faster (31 tok/s) than the $749.99 RX 9070 (24 tok/s); the 9070 read the prompt about 2.5 times faster. Decoding speed tracks memory bandwidth and software, not price.
The 24 GB Arc Pro B60 was much slower than the 16 GB RTX 5060 Ti on the 27B model (3 against 20 tok/s on Vulkan): more memory did not help when the model already fit.
On CUDA the 5060 Ti was faster still (95 and 24 tok/s on the same two models), and CUDA is not available on the Arc card.

egpu.training: Fine-tuning also fits: Qwen3-8B with NF4 QLoRA on a small slice of Tiny Shakespeare, 300 steps over 153,600 training tokens, ran at 638 tokens per second with 7,695 MiB peak GPU memory, and the evaluation loss fell from 2.65287 to 2.05897.
caveats: Prices are the article's Amazon and maker figures from 2026-11-05 and were not rechecked by us.
Everything was measured by one author on Macs running Omarchy with a patched kernel; a PC with a different port, kernel or driver may differ.
The article is about a computer you already own: the host is not in the totals.
We could not read the author's X post about it (login wall); the setup notes and the article are what we read.

source.label: Joshua Warren, "Local AI at home: a $299.99 card and a $947.95 build"

links.name: OCuLink (SFF-8611) x4 - native PCIe
links.bandwidth: PCIe 4.0 x4 = ~7.88 GB/s theoretical per direction (arithmetic); OCuLink has no speed of its own, it is whatever the host M.2/port negotiates (Gen3 x4 host = ~3.94 GB/s).
links.notes: ChargerLAB measured 6.0-6.7 GB/s through a Minisforum DEG1 (as cited by ComputingForGeeks, secondary). Next Tech and AI (YouTube transcript, excerpt) measured an Arc A770 on OCuLink: 5.68 GB/s host-to-device, 5.75 GB/s device-to-host with clpeak/Vulkan. egpu.io forum user morgwai measured DEG1 OCuLink at ~6000 MiB/s. No hot-plug: power the dock first, then boot the host, shut down before unplugging (ComputingForGeeks; M920q bifurcation GitHub thread). Cable matters: Jeff Geerling found the DEG1's bundled OCuLink cable (extra sideband wires) worked where a generic chenyang cable did not, and that straight M.2-to-OCuLink adapters without a ReDriver failed with some cards on a Pi (RX 7900 XT undetected until a ReDriver adapter was used). GPD Win Max 2 with 2x RX 6950 XT: OCuLink Gen3 vs Gen4 was 14.4 vs ~18 tok/s on a MoE paging workload (author's README).

sources.label: Local AI Master: OCuLink vs Thunderbolt 5 vs 4 (table of link rates, arithmetic, no hot-plug)
ComputingForGeeks: Best OCuLink eGPU docks and mini PCs
Jeff Geerling: not all OCuLink docks/cables are equal

links.name: Thunderbolt 3 / Thunderbolt 4 / USB4 v1 (40 Gbit/s) PCIe tunnel
links.bandwidth: Tunnel is PCIe 3.0 x4 class: ~3.94 GB/s theoretical (~32 Gbit/s). Intel requires min 32 Gbit/s PCIe on TB4. USB4 v1 PCIe tunnelling is optional in the spec and minimum USB4 data rate is 20 Gbit/s (Arch Wiki).
links.notes: Measured: morgwai (egpu.io) UT4G (ASM2464PD, USB4 v1) ~3600 MiB/s, TH3P4G3 (TB3) ~2700 MiB/s, DEG1 OCuLink ~6000 MiB/s. Next Tech and AI RX 6800 on a UT4G over USB4: 3.86 GB/s h2d / 3.82 GB/s d2h (excerpt). A Framework forum answer (single user claim) says practical TB3/TB4 eGPU maximum is ~22 Gbit/s because ~10 Gbit/s is reserved for USB3; Debian wiki says capacity 'varies from about 12 to 45 Gbps' by laptop/adapter mix. So the '22-32 Gbit/s' range is supported, with laptop implementation as the big variable. Debian wiki limitations: Nvidia Blackwell (RTX 50xx) cards are 'notorious' for problems as USB-C eGPUs; PCIe tunnelling has no GPU atomics, which disables ROCm on USB-C-attached AMD GPUs (use Vulkan). ADT-Link's own UT4G page says the dock does not support USB-only ports and 'Mac OS only supports AMD graphics cards'. Kimono Oyaji: RX 9060 XT over Thunderbolt reported link '2.5 GT/s x1' yet still beat the iGPU on 2.3GB+ models; model LOAD never completed over Thunderbolt in that author's setup, but finished in ~2 s over OCuLink (single-author, other variables changed too).

links.bandwidth: PCIe 4.0 x4 tunnel, ~7.88 GB/s theoretical (Intel quotes 64 Gbit/s for PCIe). Same PCIe bandwidth as OCuLink on paper.
links.notes: Next Tech and AI claims real-world TB5 eGPU measurements ~5.6 GB/s (excerpt of a video transcript, not verified). ComputingForGeeks: DEG2 runs TB5 and OCuLink at PCIe 4.0 x4 both. Dev.to author who 'bought Thunderbolt 5 and got USB4 40G' shows a host port labelled TB5 may only negotiate 40G; check the actual link (excerpt only). Retail TB5 docks: DEG2 ~$240-300, Sonnet 850 T5 $599.99, Razer Core X V2 ~$350 (no PSU), Gigabyte AORUS AI BOX with RTX 5060 Ti ~$700 per egpu.io guide.

links.name: M.2 / PCIe-slot to OCuLink adapters; Raspberry Pi 1-lane
links.bandwidth: Depends on host slot: a Gen4 x4 M.2 gives ~7.88 GB/s, a Gen3 x4 M.2 only ~3.94 GB/s. Raspberry Pi 5: one PCIe Gen3 lane (Geerling: ~850 MB/s peak PCIe on the Pi; ~300 MB/s from a USB3 SSD for loading).
links.notes: Geerling (Dec 2025, READ): RTX 4090 on a Pi 5 via 1 Gen3 lane lost only 2-5% of peak on LLMs when the model was resident; four RTX A5000 on one Pi (user mpsparrow) ran Llama 3 70B at 11.83 tok/s vs 12 on an Intel server (second-hand report in his post). The Pi + Minisforum DEG1 + M.2-to-OCuLink + 850W PSU build is listed at $350-400 without a GPU. ComputingForGeeks quotes Geerling's 4090 Qwen3 30B Q4 numbers as 41.05 tok/s (x1) vs 42.51 (desktop) and I confirmed the 41.05 tg128 row in his ai-benchmarks issue #43 (excerpt). One caution from the GPD README: an M.2 OCuLink adapter board that wired only 2 lanes existed; verify with lspci/GPU-Z. On mini PCs, M.2 adapters cost an SSD slot (ComputingForGeeks).

sources.label: Jeff Geerling: Big GPUs don't need big PCs

links.name: Effect on LOAD time, prompt processing and generation once resident in VRAM
links.notes: GENERATION: link barely matters if the model fits in VRAM. Geerling 4090 Qwen3 32B-class Q4 tg 41.05 (x1) vs 42.51 desktop (-3.4%, as cited by ComputingForGeeks). zephel01 (note.com, EXCERPT) cites 5-17% steady-state loss on USB4 and ~1.5-3% on OCuLink from other measurements, with a 3090 example 96 to 79.5 tok/s on Llama 3.1 8B; the 'small models lose more' pattern is plausible but I did not open the underlying source. Next Tech and AI: RX 6800 over USB4 got 44 tok/s on Qwen3 14B Q4_K_M vs 40 in a tower (excerpt). PROMPT PROCESSING: also link-insensitive when fully resident; link-bound only when layers/experts are offloaded to system RAM: gpt-oss-120b with 12 of 36 layers on GPU, pp 140 tok/s over TB3 x4 vs 304 over PCIe3 x16 (-54%), tg 2.27 vs 2.33 (egpu.io posts as quoted by ComputingForGeeks; the egpu.io thread itself mentions the benchmark but I did not see the 140/304 table). Kimono Oyaji (READ): pp on qwen3:8b 4.9GB: RX 9060 XT over Thunderbolt 2,045 tok/s vs RTX 5060 Ti on OCuLink 3,316 vs iGPU 1,217 (different GPUs, so not link-only); 1.2GB llama3.2:1b was 299 tok/s on TB but 10,668 after moving the same 9060 XT to OCuLink (author notes OS/model storage also changed, so not proof). LOAD TIME: arithmetic floors from localaimaster (27B Q4_K_M 16.2 GB: >=2.1 s on 7.88 GB/s, >=4.1 s on 4 GB/s; 70B 39 GB: ~5 s vs ~10 s), explicitly 'not measurements'. Measured OCuLink load qwen3:8b 4.9GB: 2.22 / 1.91 / 1.91 s (9060 XT), 5.22 / 2.31 / 2.32 s (5060 Ti) (Kimono Oyaji). I found NO clean measured TB-vs-OCuLink load-time table for the same card. Lane-count sweeps x1/x4/x8/x16 for llama.cpp with the model fully resident: only the Geerling x1 vs x16 result found.

multi.what: 2x RTX 3090 on one laptop, DEG1 (OCuLink) + UT4G (USB4v1), or TH3P4G3 (TB3) with UT4G daisy-chained behind it, ollama layer split, 22B-72B models
multi.result: Throughput virtually identical across both link layouts (e.g. 70B q4_K_M 17.96 vs 17.83 tok/s; qwen3 30B-A3B 107.8 vs 105.1). Author later built 2x OCuLink and got the same numbers again. GPU utilisation never above ~55% because layer split runs the cards in sequence. Daisy-chaining over TB3 was fine.
multi.caveats: Layer split only; llama.cpp tensor parallel was 'alpha' and gave no gain in the author's tries; ollama has no tensor parallel. A different poster found llama.cpp does not parallelise unless the strongest GPU is listed first in CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES. Another poster measured two GPUs slower than one on gpt-oss-120b with CPU offload.

multi.what: RTX 5090 (OCuLink) + RTX 3090 (USB4) on an EVO-X2 mini PC, 56 GB total
multi.result: Works. First dock (Minisforum DEG2) on USB4 connected for seconds, passed boltctl, then dropped out of lspci; swapping to an AOOSTAR AG02 fixed it with zero disconnects under load. 3090 ran at 99% utilisation over USB4. Same ASM2464 chip, different dock behaviour.
multi.caveats: Single-author blog, EXCERPT only; vLLM tensor parallel needs matched cards, llama.cpp --tensor-split handles mixed cards; the author's own earlier note said no 5090+3090 tok/s were found online.

multi.what: 5 GPUs on an AOOSTAR GEM 10 mini PC: 4 via M.2-to-OCuLink (x4 each), 1 via USB4 on an AOOSTAR AG02, 176 GB VRAM total (2x Quadro RTX 8000, 2x P40, 1x V100)
multi.result: Runs 235B/397B models fully GPU-resident, 24/7. OCuLink and USB4 ports do not share lanes on this host (AOOSTAR support confirmed).
multi.caveats: Boot and backup SSDs had to move to USB3 to free M.2 slots. Old datacenter cards, not a budget-friendly cost per GB claim; not tested by me.

multi.what: 2x 16GB (RX 6800 on USB4/UT4G + Arc A770 on OCuLink), 32 GB total, LM Studio Vulkan
multi.result: Gemma 4 31B Q5_K_M 13 tok/s; Qwen3.5 35B MoE Q5_K_M 50 tok/s - matched his tower. Mixed vendors work with LM Studio's even split only.
multi.caveats: Video transcript excerpt, not verified; uneven VRAM split noted; he advises hibernating before unplugging USB4 (blue screen risk).

multi.what: 2x RX 6950 XT 16GB on a GPD WIN Max 2 via 2x OCuLink Gen4 x4 for a 176B MoE with expert cache
multi.result: 17.7-19.6 tok/s decode; prefill ~18 tok/s. Needs Resizable BAR and a BIOS PFMMIO change to run two large-BAR 16GB eGPUs at once (second card allocations fail otherwise).
multi.caveats: Windows 11, custom llama.cpp PR patches; prefill is the wall.

multi.result: Default --split-mode layer is pipeline parallel and 'can tolerate slow interconnect speeds'; --split-mode tensor is experimental, mostly meaningful for NVIDIA CUDA, and is much more bottlenecked by GPU interconnect. NVIDIA's playbook says tensor parallel needs matched GPUs and recommends x8/x8 or better.
multi.caveats: So two budget eGPUs on x4 links should be run as layer split: you gain capacity, not speed (each card ~50% busy).

cost_per_gb.note: My arithmetic, not a sourced figure. eGPU overhead = UT4G $128 + cheapest 650W PSU $49.96 = $177.96 (Warren prices). Card prices: Warren Amazon for 5060 Ti; eBay used asking medians from CresvaMent Nov 5 2026 (asking, not sold) for others; 3090 uses SOLD median from GPU Sold. Host not included. Internal-GPU comparison column is the card alone (no dock/PSU), so a desktop also needs a host/PSU/case of its own.

catches: Thunderbolt/USB4 authorisation: with security level 'user' or 'secure' the dock must be authorised before PCIe tunnels exist (echo 1 > /sys/bus/thunderbolt/devices/0-1/authorized or boltctl enroll). Linux's software connection manager only offers level 'user'. Some BIOSes have a 'nopcie' level. Source: kernel.org admin guide (excerpt) and Arch Wiki (excerpt).

Hot-plug: OCuLink has none (power dock first, boot host second). USB4/TB is hot-pluggable on paper, but ADT-Link says not to unplug while a program runs; pgaleone got a kernel panic from touching the cable; Next Tech and AI recommends hibernating before disconnecting; zephel01 logged 5 USB4 drops vs 0 OCuLink drops in 200 hours (secondary, from localaimaster/egpu.io, not verified).

Linux kernel params often needed for TB/USB4: pcie_ports=native pci=assign-busses,hpbussize=0x33,realloc,hpmmiosize=...,hpmmioprefsize=16G (Arch Wiki). pgaleone also needed pcie_aspm=off, pcie_port_pm=off, iommu=pt, NVreg_DynamicPowerManagement=0 and Resizable BAR off to stop freezes with an RTX 3090 on a UT4G; took 'weeks'.
Dock quality varies on the same chip: DEG2 failed with a 3090 on USB4 where AOOSTAR AG02 (same ASM2464 family) worked at once (single report).
Cables: use the dock's bundled OCuLink cable; generic or no-ReDriver M.2 adapters can leave the card undetected (Geerling).

Power: none of DEG1/DEG2/UT4G/EG02 include a PSU. ADT-Link suggests >=450W for 3060/70-class and >=600W for 3080/4080+; Warren's $49.96 Rosewill 650W is the cheap case. 3090 spikes strained the PSU in pgaleone's build. Built-in PSU docks: AG02 (800W), Core X (650W), Sonnet 850 T5, Beelink EX (600W, Beelink only).

Partial offload is the real link-sensitive case: when MoE experts or layers sit in system RAM, prompt processing falls by around half over TB3 x4 (gpt-oss-120b 140 vs 304 tok/s) - buy enough VRAM to avoid that.
Blackwell (RTX 50xx) over USB-C eGPU is flagged as problematic on the Debian wiki, while Warren runs a 5060 Ti on USB4 successfully (on a patched kernel); mixed evidence, test before promising.
ROCm does not work on PCIe-tunnelled AMD GPUs (no atomics, Debian wiki), so Vulkan is the AMD path over USB4/TB; Warren also used Vulkan.

Backend/driver penalty is as large as the link penalty in some reports: Warren's Arc Pro B60 got 3 tok/s on a 27B and 20 on a 7B on Vulkan, whereas the public llama.cpp Vulkan scoreboard has the B60 at ~68.6 tok/s on that 7B. His 5060 Ti: 78 tok/s Vulkan vs scoreboard 93.5, 95 on his own CUDA run.
Noise/heat: not measured by any source I read; open-frame docks (DEG1) have no case fans, GPU fans only. Not found.
Resizable BAR and BIOS MMIO windows: two 16 GB cards at once needed a PFMMIO BIOS change on a GPD Win Max 2 (README); a 24 GB card needed hpmmiosize=512M in pgaleone's kernel line.
not_found: Primary-source (maker) pages for Minisforum DEG1/DEG2 and AOOSTAR were only seen as search excerpts, not opened; minisforum.com/products/deg1 returned CRAWL_NOT_FOUND.
ADT-Link R43SG and F9G prices and a plain-R43SG product page; no F9G anywhere.

A clean measured TB-vs-OCuLink MODEL LOAD time table for the same card (only OCuLink loads measured by Kimono Oyaji, plus arithmetic floors); a clean llama.cpp x1/x4/x8/x16 sweep for fully-resident models (only Geerling x1 vs x16).

Any measured tok/s for an RTX 4060 Ti 16GB, RX 7600 XT 16GB, RTX 3060 12GB, Arc B580 or Radeon PRO V620 used as an eGPU (scoreboard numbers are internal-slot Vulkan/CUDA, listed as references only). V620 appears on the Vulkan scoreboard at tg128 81.78, pp512 1595 but no price or eGPU use found.

conflict.title: The host: what the author's own setup notes say
conflict.text: The setup runs on a 16-inch M1 Max MacBook Pro under Linux, which is not a stock configuration. The author's setup notes (read by us, with captured receipts dated 2026-10-23: nvidia-smi, boltctl, PCI and kernel-log captures) say it needs a patched 7.1.12 kernel with 16K pages and a working tunnel window, a driver registry option that avoids a hard reset of the Mac, and two NVIDIA library files for Vulkan to find the card. The author measured the card over USB4 at PCIe x4 through the tunnel (the card can do x8). The Asahi Linux project said on 2026-10-28 that its own kernel does not yet support PCIe tunnelling (a post seen as an excerpt), so this is a private patched kernel, not something a stock Apple-silicon Linux install gives you. We have not reproduced any of it. On a Windows or Linux PC with USB4, Thunderbolt or OCuLink, the dock-and-card approach needs none of these patches.

sources.label: omarchy-egpu: RTX 5060 Ti setup notes (author's repository)
sources.how_seen: read page in full by us

egpu.b60_note: The article's Arc Pro B60 result (3 tok/s on a 27B model, 20 on a 7B) is far below the public llama.cpp Vulkan scoreboard, which lists the B60 at about 68.6 tok/s on the same 7B model. That points to the author's host or driver stack, not the card, so do not read it as the B60's real speed.

host_setup.title: What the author's host needed (from the setup notes)
items: A lab-patched 7.1.12 kernel with 16K pages and a working PCIe tunnel window (root-port prefetchable-window enable and identity bus addresses).

A driver registry key inside NVreg_RegistryDwords (RmForceDisableIomapWC=1). Without it, the first nvidia-smi hard-reset the Mac; with it there was no crash and no Xid error across several runs. The author infers the cause and says it was not measured for NVIDIA specifically. It also removes NVIDIA's unaligned BAR access on arm64.
For Vulkan: libEGL_nvidia.so.0 and the glvnd EGL vendor file 10_nvidia.json. Without them every Vulkan call fails and llama.cpp sees no GPU.

Two eGPUs on one tunnel: with both attached at boot, the Intel Arc card's SR-IOV BARs (56 GiB) used up the tunnel window and the second card got no address space. Running the NVIDIA card alone avoided that. Chaining the two enclosures worked with one more kernel option (hpmmioprefsize=256M).
The author's nouveau (open-source driver) route was only compiled, never run on this hardware; every measurement uses the NVIDIA open modules.

egpu.setup_discrepancy: On the same 27B model and Vulkan backend the article reports 20 tok/s generating, while the setup notes list 22.52. Both are the author's numbers from different runs and builds, so read the speed as about 20 to 23 tok/s. Splitting the model across two cards was slower (15.67) than the 5060 Ti alone.
